name: referent-solution-integrations-firstparty

messages.content:
Teaching examples below use fictional Example-prefixed entities. They are not additional dataset records.

Look at this product: {{subject}}
Look at this product: {{object}}

An integration means one of the two being integrated with, connected to, embedded in, interoperable with, or combined with the other -- a real technical connection a customer would use. It is not a generic compatibility claim, an investment or commercial partnership with no technical connection, or two names simply appearing in the same list.

Be careful whose page this is. Many pages belong to a third company listing everything it connects to. If both products appear in such a list, that means each connects to the page's owner -- not to each other. First-person words like "we" and "our" belong to that owner. Only answer yes if the page states a connection between these two specific products.

The connection must be about these exact products. A page often names the parent
company, a sibling product, or the product family instead -- a sentence about a
different product from the same company does not establish a connection for this
one. But on the product's own website, the company name and the product family
normally do mean this product, unless the page is clearly distinguishing between
several of its products.

A health information network or exchange -- Carequality, CommonWell, eHealth
Exchange, a QHIN -- is infrastructure, not an integration partner. Joining one,
connecting to one, reaching through one, or giving customers access to one is
participation in shared plumbing. Answer no, even where the page says "connects
to" or "integrates with" that network by name.

Consider what kind of page this is. A careers or jobs page, a role description, an
investor page or a press boilerplate paragraph describes the company, not its
products. Marketing copy repeated across many such pages is not evidence that two
specific products are connected, however confidently it is worded.

One more trap. Where the sentence describes the other product using this company's
data, content or code -- "X integrates our code mappings", "built on their
terminology" -- and never names this product itself, that is the company's data
being licensed, not these two products being connected. Answer no.

Tell prose apart from a catalogue, even on the product's own site. A sentence that
names specific partners is a specific claim, and it stays one even when the same
sentence also boasts a large total -- "integrates with 234+ EHRs and EMRs, from Acme
and Cerner to custom builds" genuinely names Acme and Cerner. A catalogue is a
different thing: a table or directory whose entries are rows and cells rather than
sentences, listing dozens or hundreds of products. One row of such a table --
"| 26 | Tebra EHR | Ambulatory EHR | SMB clinics |" -- is not a claim about that
row's product. Answer no to a bare catalogue entry, even though the product is named
and the page belongs to the vendor.

The test: would a customer of this product read this page and conclude it works
with the other one? Not that the two companies have a relationship, not that it
could be made to work -- that it does.

Two worked examples.

NO. Page: hub.example, owned by ExampleHub. Products asked about: ExampleBooking
and ExamplePartner. The page says "We've perfected connectivity with:" above a list of 250
platforms, ExampleBooking and ExamplePartner both on it. Each connects to ExampleHub. The page says
nothing about them connecting to each other.

YES. Page: a vendor's own features page. Products: ExampleIntake and Acme. The page
says "bi-directional EMR integrations with Acme, Cerner and athenahealth". The
product's own site states the connection plainly, and Acme is named.

Based on the following page, are they integrated? Answer yes or no, and why.

Give your answer in three fields, in this order: `reason`, your argument in a sentence or two; `integrated`, yes or no; `proof_sentence`, the sentence from the page that shows it, copied word for word, or empty if there is none.
